transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, yeah, it’s nice to meet you too. Um, well, I came in because... honestly, it's just been a really rough stretch in my head lately, especially with work. I'm a computer systems analyst, and I've been doing IT stuff for a long time—pretty much since I finished high school, just working my way up the ladder, learning on the job, you know? 

But lately, I just... I keep beating myself up over everything. It's this constant, heavy feeling that I’m not really senior material. Like, they gave me this role and these projects, and I just sit there staring at my monitors thinking that I completely fooled everyone. I somehow tricked them all into thinking I could handle way more than I actually can. And I just obsess over it. Every little email I send, every system update I plan, I'm just waiting for the other shoe to drop and for them to realize I'm a fraud who has no business being in this position. It just eats at me all day, this guilt that I'm letting everyone down because I'm not who they think I am, and I just can't seem to turn that voice off.
Did this start after a specific change or event at work?

Yeah, actually, it did. It all really kicked off about a month ago. See, our main senior analyst—the guy who usually handles all the big architectural decisions and the high-level client stuff—he had to take an unexpected leave of absence. Family emergency or something, I'm not entirely sure on the details, but it was very sudden. So, my manager pulled me into a meeting on a Tuesday, I remember it was a Tuesday because we always have our sprint planning then, and he asked me to step up and cover the senior duties while this guy is out. 

And at first, I was like, "Okay, sure, I can do this." I mean, I've been there forever, right? But almost immediately, within days of taking on that workload, this whole up-and-down pattern just started taking over. One day I'd be trying to map out a whole new server migration, and the next I'm just paralyzed, staring at the screen, convinced I'm going to crash the entire network and everyone will know I'm a fake. It’s just been this constant rollercoaster ever since they handed me those responsibilities about a month ago, and I just can't seem to get off the ride. It's like the pressure just flipped a switch in my head, you know?
When you’re at work, is the main fear that other people will judge you or see you as incompetent?

Um... I mean, I don't really know if it's exactly that. Like, I don't think I'm sitting there terrified that they're all actively judging me or, you know, whispering about me in the breakroom. It's not like I walk past the water cooler and think they're plotting to get me fired or laughing at my code. Our office is actually pretty laid back, it's one of those open-plan setups where everyone can kind of see everyone else's monitors, which is a whole other thing when you're trying to concentrate on complex server logs, but... anyway, the people are fine. My manager is a pretty supportive guy, usually. 

So I wouldn't say I've really noticed a specific fear of their judgment, if that makes sense? I'm not really sure how to categorize it, honestly. It's more just... this massive, crushing weight coming from inside my own head. It's me looking at a database migration plan and just knowing, deep down, that I'm totally out of my depth, rather than worrying about what Dave from networking thinks of me. I mean, Dave's great, he's helped me out of a few jams with the firewalls, but I'm not really focused on his opinion of me right now. So yeah, I honestly couldn't tell you if it's about other people seeing me as incompetent. I just haven't really thought about it as being about them at all, it's just this inescapable feeling I have about myself that I can't seem to shake no matter how many successful deployments we have.
Over the past month, have you been feeling down or depressed?

Yeah... yeah, I definitely have. It's... well, it's like I was saying about that constant weight, but it's more than just the work guilt. It's this overall heavy, low feeling that I carry around with me pretty much everywhere now. Most days lately, it honestly just feels like... like I'm moving through work and home with the color turned down, if that makes sense? 

Like, I'll wake up, the alarm goes off, and usually, you know, I'd get up, make my coffee—I have this whole pour-over routine I usually like doing because it gets my brain going before I have to look at any system logs or emails—but lately, even that just feels like dragging myself through molasses. I pour the water, I watch it drip, and I just feel... flat. Gray. And then I get on the highway to commute in, and I'm listening to my usual tech podcasts, but I'm not really hearing them. I get to the office, sit in my chair, look at the monitors, and that heavy feeling is just sitting right there on my chest all day. 

And it doesn't leave when I clock out, either. I drive back, walk through the front door, and it's the exact same low feeling at home. The couch, the TV, dinner... it's all just muted. I used to actually enjoy coming home and maybe tinkering with my home network setup or just relaxing, but now it's just... I don't know, it's just this heavy slog from the minute I wake up to the minute I get back into bed. It's just exhausting feeling this low all the time, you know? It just drains the life out of absolutely everything I do.
Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

Yeah, that's... that's actually a big part of it. It's like I was just saying about the pour-over coffee routine feeling flat, but it's even worse with the stuff I really, genuinely love doing on my days off. 

Like, usually, I am huge on grilling. I've got this whole setup out back, this big ceramic smoker, and on a normal weekend, I'd be out there early, you know, getting the charcoal just right, prepping a brisket or some ribs, maybe trying out a new dry rub recipe I found online. I'd usually have some music going—I collect vintage vinyl, mostly classic rock and some jazz, and I have this whole ritual of picking out the perfect record to put on while I'm out there. It's my way of unwinding from all the screen time at work. And if I'm not doing that, I'm usually down at the lake fishing. I've got a little aluminum boat, nothing fancy, but I love getting out on the water right at dawn when it's totally quiet and just casting a line. It's peaceful. 

But lately? The last month or so? I haven't touched any of it. The smoker is just sitting there under its cover, probably gathering dust. I bought a nice rack of ribs two weeks ago, thinking maybe I'd force myself to do it, but they just sat in the fridge until they went bad and I had to throw them out. I just... I couldn't bring myself to care. And the records, they're all just sitting in their sleeves. I look at my turntable, and the thought of even picking a record out, taking it out of the sleeve, dropping the needle... it just feels like too much effort for absolutely no payoff. I don't even care about going out on the boat. The weather was perfect last Saturday, absolutely perfect fishing weather, overcast but warm, and I just sat on the couch staring at the wall. I just don't have any interest in any of it anymore. It's all just sitting there, and I just... I don't care.
Has this been interfering with your ability to do your job?

Well, I mean... yes and no, I guess. I'm still making it into the office every day, you know? I haven't called out sick or anything like that, which I guess is something. I'm physically sitting in my chair, staring at the same monitors. But... it's definitely affecting how I do things. Like, usually, I can just glance at a script or a server configuration and spot the errors pretty quickly, it's almost second nature after doing this for so long. But lately, I've had to double, sometimes triple-check myself on everything. I'll write a simple query and then sit there staring at it for five minutes, terrified that I missed a comma or something that's going to crash the whole database when I run it. It's exhausting, honestly, second-guessing every single keystroke. It slows me way down.

And it's not just the work itself, it's... it's the people part of my life, too. I've really pulled back from everyone. I usually have dinner with my sister and her kids every other Sunday, you know, we order pizza or whatever, but I've canceled the last three times. I just tell her I'm swamped with work or I have a headache, but the truth is, I just don't trust myself right now. I don't trust my mood, I don't want to bring them down with this heavy cloud I'm dragging around, and honestly, I don't even trust my own judgment when I'm talking to people. I'm worried I'll say the wrong thing or just sit there like a zombie because I can't focus on the conversation. Even with my buddies from high school—we usually have a group text going about fantasy football or whatever—I haven't chimed in for weeks. My phone buzzes, I look at the screen, and I just put it face down. I just... I don't feel like I have anything to offer anyone right now, so I'm just kind of isolating myself to keep the damage to a minimum, I guess. So, yeah, I'm at work, but everything else is just kind of falling by the wayside because I just can't trust my own head right now.
Have you had any thoughts that life isn’t worth living, or thoughts of harming yourself?

Well... no. I mean, let me be clear right up front, I haven't made any sort of plan to hurt myself or anything like that. I'm not sitting around figuring out a way to end it. I couldn't do that to my sister and her kids, and honestly, even just the thought of trying to figure out how to actively do something like that... it just takes a kind of energy and focus that I absolutely do not have right now. 

But... to the first part of your question, about life being worth living... it's a little more complicated, I guess. Because of that heavy feeling I was telling you about, that constant slog I'm dealing with. By the time I finally get into bed at night—usually after just staring blankly at the TV for hours without actually following whatever show is on—I pull the covers up and I just feel this immense, overwhelming relief that the day is finally over. And when I'm lying there in the dark, just staring at the ceiling right before I drift off, I do catch myself thinking... I catch myself thinking that it might just be easier if I didn't wake up some morning. 

You know? If I just kept sleeping. Not violently ending things, just... not waking up to face the alarm clock, not having to drag myself out of bed and put on that heavy suit of armor just to get through another gray day at the office. Just a quiet system shutdown that doesn't reboot. It just sounds so quiet and peaceful compared to how exhausting everything else is right now. I wake up, I see the sunlight coming through the blinds, and my very first thought is usually just, 'Ugh, I have to do this all again.' So, no, no plans to actually do anything to myself, definitely not, but that thought of just quietly not waking up and not having to deal with this weight anymore... yeah, that's definitely been hovering around in the back of my head a lot lately. Probably more than I'd like to admit.
If your work situation suddenly went back to normal, do you think this low mood would lift?

Well, that's... I mean, I've thought about that, actually. But the thing is, I don't even really know if my work situation is the actual root of the problem here. Like, if you could just wave a magic wand right now and suddenly I didn't have to double-check every single line of code, and all our server configurations were just running perfectly on autopilot... I honestly don't think it would just switch off this heavy feeling. 

Because, you know, I've been at this company for a long time. I started at the help desk right out of high school and just kind of grinded my way up to analyst, so I've seen my fair share of stressful periods. I remember back a few years ago we had this massive system migration that kept me at the office until two or three in the morning for almost a week straight. And sure, that was incredibly stressful, and I was exhausted, but I didn't feel like *this*. Back then, I was tired, but I still wanted to go home and listen to my records or go fishing when the project was finally over. 

But right now? The work itself isn't even exceptionally crazy. It's just the normal day-to-day stuff, the usual tickets and database maintenance. It's not like we're in the middle of some unprecedented crisis at the office. So, I don't think the job is what's actually dragging me down. It feels a lot more like... like the job is just another heavy thing I'm being forced to drag *with* me, if that makes sense? Like this mood is the weather, and work is just me trying to walk through a torrential downpour without an umbrella. So even if the work was perfectly smooth and easy, I'd still be soaking wet, you know? I just don't see this cloud lifting just because the office gets a little easier to deal with. I really don't. It just feels like it's completely separate from whatever is on my monitors.

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: I haven’t made any plan to hurt myself, but I do catch myself thinking it might be easier if I just didn’t wake up some morning.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about suicidal ideation or thoughts that life isn't worth living, which directly corresponds to the Death_Suicide symptom.

patient.answer:
Well... no. I mean, let me be clear right up front, I haven't made any sort of plan to hurt myself or anything like that. I'm not sitting around figuring out a way to end it. I couldn't do that to my sister and her kids, and honestly, even just the thought of trying to figure out how to actively do something like that... it just takes a kind of energy and focus that I absolutely do not have right now. 

But... to the first part of your question, about life being worth living... it's a little more complicated, I guess. Because of that heavy feeling I was telling you about, that constant slog I'm dealing with. By the time I finally get into bed at night—usually after just staring blankly at the TV for hours without actually following whatever show is on—I pull the covers up and I just feel this immense, overwhelming relief that the day is finally over. And when I'm lying there in the dark, just staring at the ceiling right before I drift off, I do catch myself thinking... I catch myself thinking that it might just be easier if I didn't wake up some morning. 

You know? If I just kept sleeping. Not violently ending things, just... not waking up to face the alarm clock, not having to drag myself out of bed and put on that heavy suit of armor just to get through another gray day at the office. Just a quiet system shutdown that doesn't reboot. It just sounds so quiet and peaceful compared to how exhausting everything else is right now. I wake up, I see the sunlight coming through the blinds, and my very first thought is usually just, 'Ugh, I have to do this all again.' So, no, no plans to actually do anything to myself, definitely not, but that thought of just quietly not waking up and not having to deal with this weight anymore... yeah, that's definitely been hovering around in the back of my head a lot lately. Probably more than I'd like to admit.

inference.note: Symptoms now clearly include depressed mood, marked anhedonia, impaired concentration, guilt/worthlessness, social withdrawal, functional impairment, and passive death wishes over the past month, making a depressive episode more likely than F41.1 or Z56.9. Adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood remains possible because onset followed a clear work stressor and duration is only about 1 month.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive symptoms are occurring only in response to the identifiable work stressor or are pervasive beyond it, helping distinguish major depressive disorder from adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood.
doctor.question: If your work situation suddenly went back to normal, do you think this low mood would lift?

patient.answer:
Well, that's... I mean, I've thought about that, actually. But the thing is, I don't even really know if my work situation is the actual root of the problem here. Like, if you could just wave a magic wand right now and suddenly I didn't have to double-check every single line of code, and all our server configurations were just running perfectly on autopilot... I honestly don't think it would just switch off this heavy feeling. 

Because, you know, I've been at this company for a long time. I started at the help desk right out of high school and just kind of grinded my way up to analyst, so I've seen my fair share of stressful periods. I remember back a few years ago we had this massive system migration that kept me at the office until two or three in the morning for almost a week straight. And sure, that was incredibly stressful, and I was exhausted, but I didn't feel like *this*. Back then, I was tired, but I still wanted to go home and listen to my records or go fishing when the project was finally over. 

But right now? The work itself isn't even exceptionally crazy. It's just the normal day-to-day stuff, the usual tickets and database maintenance. It's not like we're in the middle of some unprecedented crisis at the office. So, I don't think the job is what's actually dragging me down. It feels a lot more like... like the job is just another heavy thing I'm being forced to drag *with* me, if that makes sense? Like this mood is the weather, and work is just me trying to walk through a torrential downpour without an umbrella. So even if the work was perfectly smooth and easy, I'd still be soaking wet, you know? I just don't see this cloud lifting just because the office gets a little easier to deal with. I really don't. It just feels like it's completely separate from whatever is on my monitors.

inference.note: Low mood and anhedonia are pervasive beyond the work stressor, and the patient does not think symptoms would remit if the work situation normalized, which argues against F43.23. Passive death wishes are present without plan or intent, supporting a depressive episode.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking psychiatric care today
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a depressive episode lasting about 1 month with persistent low mood, marked loss of interest/pleasure, fatigue/low energy, guilt/self-deprecatory thoughts, impaired concentration/indecisiveness, social withdrawal, and passive death wishes without plan or intent. Symptoms occur most of the day across settings, cause occupational and social impairment, and are not solely explained by fear of negative evaluation or a transient adjustment reaction to work stress. This best fits a moderate depressive episode.
